metadata.title: Internal Assessment (Computational Solution)
metadata.subtitle: Official coursework specification for the redesigned IB Computer Science syllabus (First Assessment May 2027). A 35-hour individual engineering project marked out of 30 marks, weighted at 30% for Standard Level and 20% for Higher Level.

paradigmShift.title: 2027 Syllabus Paradigm Shift: No External Client Required
paragraphs: A major update in the redesigned IB Computer Science curriculum is that students are NO LONGER required to have a real individual, external third-party client, or formal business contract. You do not need formal client interview transcripts, business sign-off letters, or workplace advisors.

Instead, the IA is defined as an authentic computational solution to an identified problem. The core requirement is that you identify a real-world problem or intellectual challenge that demands computational thinking, algorithmic complexity, structured data modeling, and empirical verification. The 'user' can be a user group, school club, academic peer cohort, simulated community, or even an optimization tool for personal scientific exploration.

criteria.name: Criterion A: Problem Specification
criteria.theme: Problem scenario, computational justification, user requirements & testable success criteria
criteria.description: Establish a clear, authentic problem scenario within a justifiable computational context. Define detailed functional and user requirements, analyze technical feasibility, and formulate 5 to 8 specific, measurable, and testable success criteria that anchor the entire project lifecycle.

rubric.description: The student's submission does not reach any standard described by the markband descriptors below.

The problem scenario is vaguely described or the computational context is weak or inappropriate. Solution requirements are generic, subjective, or incomplete. Success criteria are missing, purely qualitative, or untestable.

The problem scenario is thoroughly described and compellingly justified within an appropriate computational context. Requirements are comprehensive and explicitly defined. A robust set of specific, testable, and measurable success criteria is established.

deliverables.title: Authentic Problem Scenario
deliverables.description: Clear narrative describing the operational bottleneck, current manual inefficiencies, and the scope of the problem to be solved.

deliverables.title: Computational Rationale
deliverables.description: Explicit justification explaining why existing off-the-shelf software (e.g. basic spreadsheets) is unsuitable and why bespoke programmatic logic is needed.

deliverables.title: User Needs & Constraints
deliverables.description: Functional requirements, input data structures, expected system throughput, technical constraints, and target user profile.

deliverables.title: Testable Success Criteria Matrix
deliverables.description: 5 to 8 individually numbered criteria [SC1..SCn] with precise quantitative thresholds that will be tested in Criterion D and evaluated in Criterion E.

dos.title: Write Testable, Quantitative Criteria
dos.body: State measurable parameters, specific boundary numbers, response time limits, and verification methods so examiners can confirm achievement objectively.

examples.text: The system must authenticate users by hashing input passwords using SHA-256 with salting, locking the account for 300 seconds after 3 consecutive failed login attempts.
The timetable generator algorithm must resolve room allocations for 40 teachers without conflict in under 2.5 seconds, outputting a valid schedule to SQLite.

dos.title: Justify Algorithmic Need
dos.body: Demonstrate that the problem requires algorithmic complexity, automated parsing, multi-relational database integrity, or computational automation.

examples.text: A standard spreadsheet cannot enforce relational referential integrity between student prerequisite courses and course sections, resulting in manual schedule clashes that take 20+ hours each term to resolve.

donts.title: Write Vague, Subjective Descriptors
donts.body: Never use untestable subjective adjectives like 'user-friendly', 'fast', 'visually appealing', or 'secure' without measurable parameters.

examples.text: The program should be very easy to use and intuitive, and students will love using the UI. — (Pure opinion; untestable and penalized by moderators).

donts.title: Over-Scope or Invent Impossible AI Goals
donts.body: Avoid unrealistic claims that cannot be proven or developed within the 35-hour coursework allocation.

examples.text: The app will predict global cryptocurrency price movements with 100% precision using an advanced neural network. — (Unrealistic, unmeasurable, unmanageable).

criteria.examinerTip: Number each success criterion as SC-01, SC-02, up to SC-07. The external moderator will trace these exact tags directly into Criterion C (Test Strategy Matrix), Criterion D (Executed Test Logs & Screenshots), and Criterion E (Evaluation Appraisal). If an examiner sees unnumbered or narrative criteria, your coursework risks losing marks across multiple criteria due to broken coherence.

criteria.name: Criterion B: Planning
criteria.theme: Problem decomposition, development methodology, sprint roadmap & chronological task record
criteria.description: Deconstruct the overarching computational problem into modular, cohesive sub-systems. Outline a structured software development lifecycle methodology (e.g. Iterative Agile Sprints), define project milestones, and maintain a rigorous chronological task record reflecting actual technical hurdles and problem-solving decisions.

rubric.description: The student's submission does not reach any standard described by the markband descriptors below.
Problem decomposition is partial, superficial, or disorganized. The development roadmap is vague, lacking distinct milestone dates, modular sub-tasks, or chronological technical logging.

Thorough, structured decomposition of the problem into logical sub-problems and functional modules. A comprehensive, realistic development plan featuring clear milestones, task sequencing, and a detailed chronological record of development tasks.

deliverables.title: Modular Problem Decomposition
deliverables.description: Hierarchical decomposition diagram breaking the system into distinct computational layers (Data Layer, Business Logic Engine, Authentication, UI View).

deliverables.title: Development Methodology Justification
deliverables.description: Rationale for selecting an iterative development framework (e.g. 2-week agile sprints) with technical milestones linked to Success Criteria.

deliverables.title: Chronological Record of Tasks
deliverables.description: Comprehensive tabular log containing: Task ID, Sprint Date, Planned Objective, Actual Outcome, Technical Hurdle, and Resolution.

deliverables.title: Technical Dependency Inventory
deliverables.description: Audit of required frameworks, target Python runtime, third-party libraries (e.g. PyQt6, SQLite3, Matplotlib), and IDE configurations.

dos.title: Log Real Engineering Hurdles & Fixes
dos.body: Examiners want to see the iterative engineering struggle. Document authentic debugging breakthroughs, database schema alterations, and refactorings.

examples.text: Task: 'Build recursive tree search in Python' • Sprint Date: 'Oct 14, 2026 (Est: 3h, Actual: 4.5h)' • Hurdle: 'Encountered RecursionError on unbalanced binary trees with 1,200 nodes.' • Resolution: 'Implemented iterative traversal stack using deque, reducing memory overhead to O(1) auxiliary space.'

donts.title: Submit a Retrospective Fake Diary
donts.body: Examiners spot fake diaries immediately. A log that has no hurdles, smooth round hours, or generic phrases loses credibility.

examples.text: Week 1: Thought of idea. Everything went well. • Week 2: Coded the entire program without errors. • Week 3: Tested and finished. — (Zero technical specificity; capped at 1-2 marks).

criteria.examinerTip: Ensure your decomposition diagram explicitly separates concerns. If you present a diagram with only 2 boxes ('Code' and 'Database'), you will be capped at 1–2 marks. Show distinct modules: Data Model, Business Engine, Validation Filter, Presentation Layer, and File I/O.

criteria.name: Criterion C: System Overview
criteria.theme: System architecture models, algorithmic flowcharts & pseudocode, UI wireframes, 3-tier testing strategy
criteria.description: Provide architectural system modeling (UML class diagrams, ER diagrams, data dictionaries), formal algorithm representations (standard IB flowcharts and pseudocode), annotated UI wireframes, and a comprehensive 3-tier planned testing strategy (Normal, Boundary, Abnormal data) mapped directly to Criterion A success criteria.

rubric.description: The student's submission does not reach any standard described by the markband descriptors below.
System models are missing or severely incomplete. Algorithms are represented informally or superficially. UI mockups are absent. Testing strategy is missing or lacks clear data categories.
Adequate system modeling provided (e.g. basic UML or database diagram). Core algorithms represented via flowcharts or pseudocode. UI wireframes present. Basic test strategy outlined with normal data.

Comprehensive, professional system modeling (complete UML class diagram with visibility and relationships, database ER diagram, data dictionary). Detailed algorithmic designs using standard pseudocode and flowcharts for non-trivial logic. Annotated UI wireframes. Rigorous 3-tier testing strategy covering normal, boundary, and abnormal test data mapped directly to Criterion A success criteria.

deliverables.title: Standard UML Class Diagram
deliverables.description: Complete OOP class diagram showing class names, private/public attributes, method signatures, return types, inheritance, and multiplicities.

deliverables.title: Relational ER Diagram & Data Dictionary
deliverables.description: Entity-relationship schema with primary/foreign keys and data dictionary defining field types, lengths, validation rules, and default values.

deliverables.title: Algorithm Flowcharts & IB Pseudocode
deliverables.description: Formal algorithmic specifications for core custom routines (sorting, graph traversal, recursive rebalancing, validation parsers).

deliverables.title: Planned 3-Tier Testing Matrix Table
deliverables.description: Structured table pre-planning every test case with: Test ID, Criterion ID, Test Type (Normal, Boundary, Abnormal), Exact Input Data, and Expected Outcome.

dos.title: Plan Normal, Boundary & Abnormal Data
dos.body: A test plan that only tests valid inputs cannot score above 4 marks. Include boundary limits and deliberately invalid inputs to verify defensive exception handling.

examples.text: Test T1 (Normal): Input 'Passw0rd123!' -> Auth success, redirect to dashboard. • Test T2 (Boundary): Input password with exactly 8 chars -> Accepted. • Test T3 (Boundary): Input password with 7 chars -> Error 'Min 8 chars required.' • Test T4 (Abnormal): Input SQL injection "' OR '1'='1" -> Sanitized and blocked.

donts.title: Draw Informal Sketches or Box Dumps
donts.body: Do not use generic unformatted boxes with no method parameters, attribute types, or arrows. Hand-drawn unreadable sketches are penalized.

examples.text: Box with just 'User' pointing to 'Database' with an unlabelled line. No method signatures like +login(u: str, p: str): bool, no primary keys. — (Instantly caps Criterion C at 2 marks).

criteria.examinerTip: Remember: Criterion C is the plan, not the result. Do not paste screenshots of test results in Criterion C! Criterion C contains the blank test matrix with planned inputs and expected outcomes. The actual screenshots and executed results belong in Criterion D.

criteria.name: Criterion D: Development & Algorithmic Complexity
criteria.theme: Working computational solution, algorithmic complexity, technical justifications & empirical test evidence
criteria.description: The central core of the IA carrying 40% of the entire grade. Candidates must prove non-trivial algorithmic mastery, OOP modular structure, defensive programming, and rigorous technical decision-making. Includes annotated excerpts of 4–6 core algorithms and empirical test execution evidence (actual screenshots and logs) validating every single success criterion.

rubric.description: The software demonstrates limited functionality. Trivial programming techniques are used (linear procedural scripts, basic if-else logic). Code lacks modularity. Technical decisions are unjustified. Testing evidence is minimal or incomplete.

The solution is partially functioning with moderate complexity. Basic modular structures are implemented. Code excerpts are present with minimal annotations. Testing evidence covers some criteria but lacks boundary or abnormal cases.

The computational solution is fully functional and exhibits sound algorithmic complexity (custom OOP classes, search/sort, structured file or database persistence). Modular code with clear structure. Sound justification of technical decisions. Good testing evidence validating most success criteria.

High-level computational solution demonstrating advanced algorithmic complexity (custom recursion, dynamic programming, custom tree/graph algorithms, relational queries, defensive validation). Elegant, modular OOP architecture. Thoroughly annotated code excerpts justifying technical trade-offs. Exhaustive empirical testing evidence (screenshots, terminal logs, database state changes) confirming ALL Criterion A success criteria across normal, boundary, and abnormal cases.

deliverables.title: Evidence of Algorithmic Complexity
deliverables.description: Demonstration of non-trivial computational thinking: recursive algorithms, custom searching/sorting, multi-dimensional data structures, OOP inheritance, or SQL relational joins.

deliverables.title: Annotated Code Excerpts (4–6 Samples)
deliverables.description: High-resolution code snippets with line-by-line annotations explaining algorithm mechanics, defensive exceptions, and time/space complexity.

deliverables.title: Technical Decision Justifications
deliverables.description: Explicit rationale explaining why specific architectures, algorithms, and data persistence models were chosen over alternatives.

deliverables.title: Completed Testing Table with Screenshots
deliverables.description: Empirical proof: Executed test cases matching Criterion C test plan with actual inputs, outputs, Pass/Fail badges, and indexed screenshot references.

dos.title: Write Custom Algorithmic Logic
dos.body: Examiners grade YOUR algorithmic logic, not external library calls. Write custom traversal, mathematical heuristics, sorting filters, or recursive parsers.

examples.text:
# Lines 45-62: Recursive QuickSort with Median-of-Three Pivot
def _quick_sort(self, records, low, high):
    if low < high:
        pivot_idx = self._partition(records, low, high)
        self._quick_sort(records, low, pivot_idx - 1)
        self._quick_sort(records, pivot_idx + 1, high)
# Annotation: Chosen over standard BubbleSort to achieve O(n log n) average time complexity when handling up to 5,000 transaction records (SC-02).

dos.title: Provide Screenshot Evidence for Every Test
dos.body: Every row in your testing table must have an embedded screenshot proving that the software actually ran and handled the test case.

examples.text: Test T3 (Boundary: password length = 7) -> Expected: Error dialogue -> Actual: UI dialogue displayed: 'Password must contain at least 8 characters' -> Status: PASS • [See Figure D.4: UI boundary warning screenshot].

donts.title: Rely on Black-Box One-Liners
donts.body: If your program just calls data.sort_values() or calls a third-party AI API with zero student-written logic, you will be penalized heavily in algorithmic complexity.

examples.text:
def do_everything():
    response = openai.ChatCompletion.create(...) # 95% of project
    print(response)
(Fatal flaw: zero candidate algorithmic complexity demonstrated; marks capped at 3/12).

donts.title: Dump Unannotated Source Code
donts.body: Never paste 30 pages of raw code without line-by-line annotations. Examiners will not read raw dumps; they only score annotated snippets.

examples.text: Pasting 1,500 lines of boilerplate UI button positioning code or standard getter/setter properties without explaining algorithmic significance.

criteria.examinerTip: Criterion D is where students gain or lose the most marks in the entire diploma. To reach 10–12 marks, you must show both algorithmic depth (demonstrating why your code is computationally non-trivial) and empirical testing validity (proving with screenshots that boundary and abnormal inputs are properly caught).

criteria.name: Criterion E: Evaluation & Future Recommendations
criteria.theme: Systematic appraisal against Criterion A success criteria, authentic user/peer feedback & technical future extensions
criteria.description: Conduct a rigorous, objective evaluation of the completed software mapped directly back to every single Criterion A success criterion. Analyze empirical test results honestly, integrate authentic peer/user evaluation feedback, and propose concrete, technically grounded recommendations for future iterations.

rubric.description: The student's submission does not reach any standard described by the markband descriptors below.

Evaluation against success criteria is superficial or partial. Feedback from users/peers is absent, subjective, or invented. Recommendations for future improvements are vague, cosmetic, or non-technical.

Systematic, objective evaluation of each success criterion from Criterion A supported by empirical test results. Meaningful, authentic user or peer feedback is analyzed. Concrete, technically feasible recommendations for future improvements are proposed.

deliverables.title: Success Criteria Evaluation Matrix
deliverables.description: Comprehensive table auditing each criterion [SC-01..SC-07] with status (Fully Met, Partially Met, Unmet) and explicit cross-references to Criterion D test evidence.

deliverables.title: Critical Analysis of Limitations
deliverables.description: Objective discussion of software edge cases, performance bottlenecks, computational inefficiencies, and scalability constraints.

deliverables.title: Authentic User & Peer Feedback
deliverables.description: Documented qualitative and quantitative feedback collected from real users, testers, or student peers running the software on different devices.

deliverables.title: Justified Technical Recommendations
deliverables.description: 3 to 5 realistic, technically detailed architectural improvements (e.g. database indexing, async networking, concurrency management) for version 2.0.

dos.title: Be Honest About Limitations
dos.body: Examiners award high marks for critical honesty. Acknowledging partially met criteria and explaining technical reasons shows superior academic maturity.

examples.text: SC-04 (CSV Batch Import): Partially Met. While the parser successfully processes standard UTF-8 files up to 2,000 rows, it crashes on Windows-1252 encoded strings with accented characters (Test D.12). A dedicated encoding auto-detection filter using chardet should be implemented.

dos.title: Write Actionable Technical Future Work
dos.body: Propose concrete software engineering upgrades with named libraries, data structures, or algorithms.

examples.text: Recommendation 1: Replace synchronous SQLite transactions with an asynchronous connection pool via aiosqlite and introduce a B-tree composite index on (student_id, term_date) to reduce timetable query latency from 850ms to <50ms.

donts.title: Write Blanket Self-Praise
donts.body: Never write that your program is flawless or that zero improvements are needed. This is an immediate red flag for examiners.

examples.text: My project was a complete success with 100% perfection. All features work amazingly and the user said it was the best software they had ever seen. — (Immediate deduction to 1-2 marks).

donts.title: Give Trivial or Cosmetic Suggestions
donts.body: Avoid superficial wishes like changing button colors or adding generic animations.

examples.text: In the future I would make the background blue, add some sound effects, and make it look prettier. — (Zero technical value).

criteria.examinerTip: Every single criterion listed in Criterion A must appear in the Criterion E evaluation matrix. If you wrote 7 success criteria in A, there must be 7 rows evaluated in E. If a criterion was not met, state 'Unmet / Partially Met' and explain why; examiners reward critical reflection!

exemplars.name: Example 1
exemplars.title: Birthday Card Generator
exemplars.techStack: Python 3 • Canvas / Pillow • Template Engine • File Export
exemplars.summary: An interactive desktop solution that generates personalized digital and printable birthday greeting cards using customizable graphic templates, dynamic typography, and batch PDF/image export.
exemplars.highlight: Demonstrates clear OOP inheritance, modular canvas coordinate math, and structured input validation for custom dimensions and color palettes.

criteriaFocus.note: Clearly specifies card dimension constraints, DPI resolution requirements, and font fallback criteria.
Includes detailed UML class hierarchy for template elements (TextLayer, ImageLayer, ShapeLayer).
Shows algorithmic manipulation of pixel buffers and automated coordinate scaling.

exemplars.name: Example 2
exemplars.title: Quiz Game
exemplars.techStack: Python 3 • JSON Question Banks • State Machine • Timed Logic
exemplars.summary: A modular quiz application with multiple question types, dynamic difficulty weighting, timed countdown mechanics, randomized question pools, and persistent high-score tracking.
exemplars.highlight: Exemplifies clean state machine design separating gameplay state from rendering, plus structured JSON parsing with defensive schema checks.

criteriaFocus.note: Defines explicit testable thresholds for question timing, scoring multipliers, and leaderboards.
Comprehensive state transition diagram and data structure dictionary for question objects.
Features non-trivial Fisher-Yates shuffle implementations and streak calculation algorithms.

exemplars.name: Example 3
exemplars.title: Chat Room
exemplars.techStack: Python 3 • Socket Programming • Multi-Threading • Packet Protocol
exemplars.summary: A multi-client TCP/IP chat system featuring asynchronous multi-threading, custom messaging protocol headers, user authentication, and broadcast channels.
exemplars.highlight: Implements non-trivial network concurrency, thread safety mechanisms (locks/mutexes), and formatted packet serialization.

criteriaFocus.note: Specifies packet delivery latency targets, concurrent client limits, and disconnect recovery behaviors.
Sequence diagrams illustrating TCP handshake, broadcast dissemination, and client disconnection flow.
Thread lifecycle management, socket exception handling, and buffer boundary parsing.

exemplars.name: Example 4
exemplars.title: Car Management System
exemplars.techStack: Python 3 • SQLite3 • Relational Schema • Tkinter / CustomTkinter
exemplars.summary: A commercial fleet tracking and service management tool providing full relational CRUD capabilities, mileage tracking, service alert schedules, and billing report generation.
exemplars.highlight: Exemplary relational schema with primary and foreign keys, parameterized SQL queries preventing injection, and robust input validation.

criteriaFocus.note: Clearly defines business requirements for maintenance intervals, inventory filters, and invoice totals.
Third-normal-form (3NF) Entity-Relationship diagram and exhaustive 3-tier test plan.
Complex SQL JOIN queries, date calculation heuristics, and automated report compilation.

exemplars.name: Example 5
exemplars.title: Currency Converter
exemplars.techStack: Python 3 • REST API / Offline Caching • Numeric Precision • GUI
exemplars.summary: A currency conversion utility supporting multi-currency cross-rate arithmetic, historical trend visual graphs, commission calculation, and offline cached fallback exchange tables.
exemplars.highlight: Demonstrates defensive programming for floating-point rounding precision, HTTP connection fallbacks, and real-time input sanitization.

criteriaFocus.note: Defines rounding precision criteria (e.g. 4 decimal places) and offline timeout handling thresholds.
Data dictionary covering conversion factors, ISO currency codes, and cache expiry algorithms.
Arbitrage-free triangular conversion algorithms and defensive exception recovery.

exemplars.name: Example 6
exemplars.title: IB Timetable
exemplars.techStack: Python 3 • Backtracking / Heuristic Solver • 2D Matrices • CSV Export
exemplars.summary: A sophisticated automated timetable scheduler that assigns classes, teachers, and rooms while strictly resolving complex time clash constraints and teacher availability matrices.
exemplars.highlight: High algorithmic sophistication featuring backtracking constraint-satisfaction algorithms, multidimensional array indexing, and conflict diagnostics.

criteriaFocus.note: Measurable success criteria specify max teacher continuous periods, room capacity limits, and solve-time benchmarks.
Algorithm pseudocode and trace tables analyzing worst-case search space complexity.
Recursive backtracking algorithm with pruning heuristics to prevent infinite search loops.

exemplars.name: Example 7
exemplars.title: Trip Organizer
exemplars.techStack: Python 3 • Hierarchical JSON • Sorting / Filtering • Report Generator
exemplars.summary: An itinerary planner and travel expense budget optimizer allowing travelers to plan multi-day schedules, calculate shared trip costs, and optimize transport routes.
exemplars.highlight: Clean separation of business logic from UI, multi-key sorting heuristics, and comprehensive test documentation covering diverse trip configurations.

criteriaFocus.note: Quantifiable criteria for per-day expense limits, currency balance reconciliation, and itinerary exports.
Modular component decomposition diagrams and exhaustive validation test tables.
Multi-parameter sorting and dynamic cost aggregation across nested activity arrays.

exemplars.name: Example 8
exemplars.title: Flappy Bird
exemplars.techStack: Python 3 • Pygame • Velocity / Acceleration Physics • Collision Detection
exemplars.summary: A customized arcade simulation game featuring discrete-time physics integration (gravity, jump velocity), dynamic obstacle generation, AABB collision detection, and session persistence.
exemplars.highlight: Demonstrates game-loop architecture, real-time event queue dispatching, math calculations for bounding box collisions, and frame-rate smoothing.

criteriaFocus.note: Specifies frame-rate targets (60 FPS), gravity acceleration coefficients, and collision pixel tolerances.
Main loop activity diagrams and mathematical formulations for bounding box overlap detection.
Delta-time physics integration, procedural pipe gap generation, and high-score file encryption.

sections.title: Paradigm Shift: No External Client Required
sections.description: Why third-party client interviews and business contracts are no longer required, shifting focus entirely to authentic computational problem solving.

sections.title: Criteria A & B: Specification & Agile Roadmap
sections.description: Formulating 5 to 8 quantitative, testable success criteria [SC-01..SC-07] and decomposing problems into structured modules with an agile record of tasks.

sections.title: Criterion C: System Architecture & Testing Strategy
sections.description: Constructing UML class diagrams, database ER schemas, data flow models, and planning a rigorous 3-tier test matrix (normal, boundary, abnormal).

sections.title: The Redesigned 2027 Internal Assessment Architecture
paragraphs: The Internal Assessment (IA) for the redesigned International Baccalaureate Diploma Programme (IB DP) Computer Science curriculum—first assessed in May 2027—is an individual computational project that challenges students to solve a genuine problem through algorithmic thinking and software development.

Unlike the legacy syllabus (which was marked out of 34 marks and mandated external third-party client interviews), the 2027 specification is marked out of 30 marks across five unified criteria (A through E). It accounts for 30% of the final grade at Standard Level (SL) and 20% of the final grade at Higher Level (HL), representing approximately 35 hours of instructional and development time.

summaryTable.scope: Problem specification, computational context, user requirements & success criteria
Problem decomposition, development methodology & chronological task logging
System architecture modeling, algorithms, UI wireframes & testing strategy
Working solution, algorithmic complexity, technical decisions & test evidence
Systematic evaluation against success criteria, user feedback & future extensions

sections.title: The Client Requirement Dispelled: Authentic Problem Solving
paragraphs: A widespread point of confusion among IB students relates to the requirement of an external 'client'. Under previous curriculum guides, candidates had to identify an external third-party individual or small business and conduct recorded interviews.

In the redesigned 2027 curriculum, an external client is NO LONGER strictly mandated. The IB recognized that finding authentic commercial clients created artificial barriers and resulted in scripted interactions. The 2027 IA refocuses squarely on authentic computational problem-solving.

domains.name: School / Community Operational Tools
domains.description: Automated scheduling engines, library asset trackers, sports tournament brackets with conflict resolution.

domains.name: Scientific & Mathematical Simulators
domains.description: Orbital mechanics visualizers, epidemiological transmission models, ecological predator-prey systems.

domains.name: Algorithmic & Educational Platforms
domains.description: Interactive sorting/graph algorithm visualizers, adaptive flashcard engines utilizing spaced repetition heuristics.

domains.name: Data Processing & Analytics Utilities
domains.description: Relational data management systems with custom filtering, data sanitization, and automated PDF report generation.

domains.name: Game Engineering with Algorithmic AI
domains.description: Strategy board games (e.g. Chess, Connect Four) powered by Minimax algorithms with alpha-beta pruning.

sections.title: The Golden Chain of Consistency (The Core Examiner Principle)
paragraphs: According to official IB examiner subject reports and senior teacher syllabus benchmarks, the single most critical factor in achieving a Grade 7 (26–30 marks) is maintaining an unbroken chain of consistency across all five criteria. The success criteria formulated in Criterion A must drive every subsequent phase of the project:
sections.takeaway: If an examiner identifies a criterion tested in D that was never specified in A, or if Criterion E evaluates features never tested in D, your coursework is penalized for fragmented planning. Ensure that every success criterion has an identical ID (e.g. SC-01 through SC-07) maintained seamlessly throughout the document.

sections.title: Technical Stack, Language Selection & Data Persistence
paragraphs: The IB Diploma Programme does not mandate a specific programming language. However, the chosen language must support object-oriented programming (OOP) principles, structured data manipulation, and non-trivial algorithmic techniques.

Python 3.x is the primary language recommended at Emirates International School Meadows due to its expressive syntax, comprehensive standard library, robust database bindings (sqlite3), and GUI frameworks (PyQt6, Tkinter, CustomTkinter). Java and C# are equally acceptable if students possess advanced fluency.

Projects that store data purely in temporary RAM variables (e.g. basic Python dictionaries that reset when the window closes) will be heavily capped in Criterion D. A top-band computational solution must implement structured data persistence (Relational SQLite or hierarchical JSON/CSV).

sections.title: Academic Integrity & Generative AI Regulations
paragraphs: Emirates International School Meadows enforces the official IB Academic Integrity Policy across all coursework stages. With the rise of Large Language Models (LLMs) and code assistants (ChatGPT, GitHub Copilot, Claude), candidates must strictly adhere to the following rules:

rules.title: Original Code Authorship
rules.description: All core algorithmic logic, data models, and business logic must be authored directly by the candidate. Using AI to generate entire functions, classes, or documentation violates IB regulations.

rules.title: AI Assistance Declaration
rules.description: If generative AI is used for conceptual brainstorming, troubleshooting a syntax error, or syntax referencing, the interaction must be transparently cited in an appendix (specifying the tool, version, prompt, and date).

rules.title: Third-Party Library Attribution
rules.description: Using open-source libraries (e.g. Pygame, NumPy, PyQt, bcrypt) is fully permitted, but they must be explicitly cited in a dedicated library declaration table in Criterion D.

sections.title: Coursework Assembly & Final Submission Checklist
items: Single PDF Document: The complete written coursework (Criteria A through E) must be compiled into a single PDF document.
Word Count Guidelines: The recommended word limit is approximately 2,000 to 3,000 words across all criteria (excluding code listings, UML diagrams, test data tables, and bibliographies).
Numbered Success Criteria: Ensure all criteria in Criterion A are tagged (e.g. SC-01) and traced verbatim into Criteria C, D, and E.
Empirical Test Screenshots: Verify that every row in your Criterion D test execution table includes an accompanying screenshot showing actual program output.
Anonymity Standards: Remove all student names and school names from the document header and body, retaining only your candidate session code.
